concepts.name: Solar Constant and Insolation at Top of Atmosphere
key_dimensions: Definition and value of solar constant (~1361 W/m²) vs. commonly cited ~1.94 cal/cm²/min — distinction and trap
Difference between solar constant (extraterrestrial) and insolation received at Earth's surface after atmospheric losses
Why Earth's average insolation is ~342 W/m² (one-fourth of solar constant) — geometric reasoning with spherical Earth
Variability due to Earth-Sun distance (perihelion vs. aphelion) and its limited effect on seasons

concepts.name: Albedo: Concept, Values, and Climatic Significance
key_dimensions: Definition of albedo and Earth's average planetary albedo (~30%) — what contributes to it (clouds ~20%, surface ~10%)
Comparative albedo values: fresh snow (~80-90%), forest (~10-15%), ocean (~6-10%), desert (~25-30%) — common exam trap on ranking
Role of albedo in feedback mechanisms: ice-albedo feedback (positive feedback loop) and its role in climate change
Distinction between albedo and emissivity — UPSC often conflates these in options

concepts.name: Disposition of Incoming Solar Radiation (Insolation Budget — 100 Units Framework)
key_dimensions: Standard breakdown: ~30 units reflected (albedo), ~19 units absorbed by atmosphere/clouds, ~51 units absorbed by Earth's surface
Role of clouds in both reflecting (shortwave) and absorbing (longwave) radiation — dual role is a frequent trap
Difference between scattering, reflection, and absorption — selective processes for different wavelengths
Why only 51% reaches the surface yet Earth maintains energy balance — linkage to longwave re-emission

concepts.name: Terrestrial Radiation and Longwave Emission
key_dimensions: Earth absorbs shortwave (solar) radiation and emits longwave (infrared) radiation — Wien's Displacement Law linkage
Stefan-Boltzmann Law: relationship between temperature and emitted radiation — conceptual application, not mathematical
Why Earth emits in infrared spectrum (peak ~10 micrometers) vs. Sun emitting in visible spectrum (peak ~0.5 micrometers)
Distinction between terrestrial radiation and atmospheric radiation (counter-radiation) — often confused in options

concepts.name: Greenhouse Effect: Natural vs. Enhanced
key_dimensions: Mechanism: GHGs transparent to shortwave, opaque to longwave — selective absorption creating warming (~33°C natural warming)
Key GHGs by warming potential vs. by concentration: CO₂ (most abundant anthropogenic), water vapor (most abundant natural), CH₄, N₂O, O₃ — ranking trap
Global Warming Potential (GWP): CH₄ (25x), N₂O (298x), SF₆ (22,800x) vs. CO₂ baseline — UPSC frequently tests this
Distinction between greenhouse effect (natural, necessary) and enhanced greenhouse effect (anthropogenic, problematic) — definitional trap

concepts.name: Heat Budget Equilibrium: Earth's Energy Balance at 0 Net
key_dimensions: Earth receives ~342 W/m² and emits ~342 W/m² in equilibrium — concept of radiative balance
How the 51 units absorbed by surface are balanced: ~23 units via latent heat, ~9 units via sensible heat (conduction/convection), ~19 units via longwave radiation to atmosphere
Difference between instantaneous imbalance (day/night, seasons) and long-term equilibrium — Earth's current energy imbalance due to climate change (~0.6 W/m²)
Role of oceans as heat reservoirs in maintaining equilibrium — thermal inertia concept

concepts.name: Latent Heat Transfer as a Component of Heat Budget
key_dimensions: Latent heat of evaporation (~23 units in budget) vs. sensible heat (~9 units) — relative importance often reversed in options
Mechanism: evaporation from surface absorbs heat, condensation in atmosphere releases heat — energy transfer without temperature change
Role of latent heat in driving atmospheric circulation (Hadley cells, monsoon systems)
Distinction between latent heat and sensible heat flux — Bowen Ratio concept for land vs. ocean differences

concepts.name: Atmospheric Window and Selective Absorption by GHGs
key_dimensions: Atmospheric window (8–13 micrometers): wavelengths that escape directly to space without absorption — why Earth loses heat
Water vapor and CO₂ absorption bands — CO₂ absorbs at 15 micrometers, water vapor across broad spectrum
Ozone absorption of UV radiation (stratospheric) vs. IR absorption (tropospheric) — dual role of ozone
Closing of atmospheric window by increased CO₂/CH₄ — mechanism of enhanced greenhouse effect; trap: ozone hole ≠ greenhouse effect

concepts.name: Differential Heating of Land and Water: Specific Heat Capacity
key_dimensions: Specific heat capacity of water (~4x that of land) — why oceans heat/cool slowly (maritime climate) vs. land (continental climate)
Penetration depth: solar radiation penetrates water to depth (mixing), land absorbs only at surface — amplifying land's temperature extremes
Consequences: diurnal and seasonal temperature range differences between coastal and interior regions
Role in monsoon genesis: differential heating between Indian subcontinent and Indian Ocean driving pressure gradient

concepts.name: Insolation Variation with Latitude: Controls and Patterns
key_dimensions: Three geometric reasons for latitudinal variation: angle of incidence (obliquity), path length through atmosphere, duration of daylight
Why tropics receive more annual insolation than poles — even though poles get 24-hour sunlight in summer (angle effect dominates)
Equinox vs. solstice insolation patterns — on equinox, equator gets maximum; on solstice, respective tropic gets maximum — trap
Relationship between insolation distribution and global temperature belts (torrid, temperate, frigid zones)

concepts.name: Counter-Radiation (Atmospheric Back Radiation) and Its Role
key_dimensions: Atmosphere absorbs terrestrial longwave radiation and re-emits ~2/3 back to Earth (counter-radiation) and ~1/3 to space
Counter-radiation explains why nights are warmer under cloudy skies — clouds act as blanket trapping longwave radiation
Quantitative balance: Earth surface receives more radiation from atmosphere (~333 W/m²) than directly from Sun (~161 W/m²) — counterintuitive fact
Role of counter-radiation in preventing extreme cold at night — comparison: Moon (no atmosphere) has extreme diurnal temperature range (~300°C)

concepts.name: Heat Budget Variation by Latitude: Surplus and Deficit Zones
key_dimensions: Tropics (0°–35°): heat surplus (insolation absorbed > outgoing longwave radiation emitted)
Polar regions (>35°–40°): heat deficit (more longwave emitted than insolation received) — exact latitude of balance varies by hemisphere
Mechanism of redistribution: atmospheric circulation (winds, ~40%) and oceanic circulation (ocean currents, ~60%) — relative proportion is a UPSC trap
Without redistribution, tropics would continuously heat and poles would continuously cool — this drives global circulation systems

concepts.name: Role of Ocean Currents in Heat Budget Redistribution
key_dimensions: Poleward heat transport by warm currents (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio) — moderating climates of Western Europe and NW Pacific coasts
Cold currents absorbing heat from atmosphere in tropical regions, reducing temperatures of adjacent landmasses (Benguela, California currents)
Thermohaline circulation as global heat conveyor belt — AMOC and its potential disruption under climate change
Ocean heat content as metric for monitoring Earth's energy imbalance — 90%+ of excess heat stored in oceans

concepts.name: Conduction and Convection in Atmospheric Heat Transfer
key_dimensions: Conduction: molecule-to-molecule transfer — significant only at surface-atmosphere interface (thin boundary layer), poor conductor air
Convection: vertical heat transfer through rising air masses — more important than conduction in atmosphere; drives lapse rate
Advection: horizontal transfer of heat by wind — responsible for warm/cold waves, maritime air penetration into continents
Distinction: conduction (no mass movement), convection (vertical mass movement), advection (horizontal mass movement) — definitional trap

concepts.name: Lapse Rate Types and Their Relationship to Heat Budget
key_dimensions: Normal/Environmental Lapse Rate (ELR): ~6.5°C/1000m — average observed; not constant, varies with moisture and season
Dry Adiabatic Lapse Rate (DALR): 10°C/1000m for unsaturated air — no heat exchange with surroundings (adiabatic)
Saturated Adiabatic Lapse Rate (SALR): ~6°C/1000m (variable) — lower due to latent heat release during condensation; trap: SALR < DALR
Atmospheric stability conditions: ELR < SALR (stable), ELR > DALR (absolutely unstable), SALR < ELR < DALR (conditionally unstable)

concepts.name: Temperature Inversion: Types, Causes, and Implications
key_dimensions: Definition: temperature increases with altitude (reversal of normal lapse rate) — acts as a lid on convection and pollutant dispersal
Types: surface/radiation inversion (clear nights, calm winds), subsidence inversion (high-pressure systems, trade wind inversion), frontal inversion
Geographic examples: California's temperature inversion causing smog, Arctic temperature inversion, trade wind inversion limiting rainfall in subtropical deserts
Role in heat budget: inversion layers trap heat near surface (radiation inversion warms surface) vs. subsidence inversion (upper warming, surface cooling)

concepts.name: Urban Heat Island Effect as a Micro-Scale Heat Budget Modification
key_dimensions: Mechanism: reduced albedo (dark surfaces), reduced evapotranspiration (impervious surfaces), waste heat from human activities, reduced sky view factor
Urban areas 1–3°C warmer than surrounding rural areas — affects local precipitation patterns (more convective rainfall downwind)
Heat budget modification: urban areas absorb more shortwave, emit more longwave, have altered Bowen Ratio (more sensible, less latent heat)
Mitigation strategies: green roofs, cool pavements (high albedo), urban forests — linkage to sustainable urban planning (UPSC current affairs angle)

concepts.name: Ozone Layer and Its Role in Heat Budget (UV Absorption)
key_dimensions: Stratospheric ozone absorbs UV-B and UV-C radiation (240–320 nm) — heats stratosphere, explaining stratospheric temperature increase with altitude
Stratospheric warming vs. tropospheric warming — ozone depletion cools stratosphere while GHGs warm troposphere — opposite trends are diagnostic
Distinction: ozone hole ≠ greenhouse effect — common confusion in UPSC options; ozone depletion affects UV, not significantly IR
Antarctic ozone hole seasonality (spring maximum depletion) — role of Polar Stratospheric Clouds (PSCs) in catalytic ozone destruction

concepts.name: Aerosols and Dust: Direct and Indirect Effects on Heat Budget
key_dimensions: Direct effect: scattering and absorbing solar radiation — net cooling (sulfate aerosols scatter) or warming (black carbon/soot absorbs) — sign depends on type
Indirect effect: aerosols as Cloud Condensation Nuclei (CCN) — more CCN → more numerous, smaller droplets → brighter clouds (higher albedo) → cooling (Twomey effect)
Aerosol masking: anthropogenic aerosols partially offset GHG warming — 'aerosol masking' hypothesis and implications for rapid decarbonization
Volcanic aerosols (SO₂ → sulfate) causing global cooling (e.g., Mt. Pinatubo 1991 caused ~0.5°C cooling for 1–2 years) — short-term vs. long-term effect

concepts.name: Milankovitch Cycles and Long-Term Heat Budget Variation
key_dimensions: Three orbital parameters: eccentricity (~100,000-year cycle), axial tilt/obliquity (~41,000-year cycle), precession (~26,000-year cycle) — name, duration, effect distinctions
Eccentricity affects total annual insolation received; obliquity affects seasonal contrast; precession affects timing of seasons relative to orbit
Linkage to glacial-interglacial cycles — Milankovitch cycles as 'pacemaker' of ice ages but alone insufficient (amplified by GHG and ice-albedo feedbacks)
Current orbital configuration: low eccentricity, moderate obliquity — why we are in an interglacial and why Milankovitch cycles cannot explain current rapid warming
